legend: A small tissue fragment consisting of large cells with abundant, vacuolated cytoplasm and large epithelioid nuclei with significant variation in nuclear size (Pap).

Large tumour cells contain intracytoplasmic lumina containing red blood cells and neutrophils. A mitosis can be seen in the bottom of the field; because these are rarely seen in epithelioid haemangioendothelioma, their presence can suggest the possibility of an epithelioid angiosarcoma (Pap).
A loosely cohesive tissue fragment consisting of epithelioid cells with abundant cytoplasm containing small vacuoles, along with red blood cells and neutrophils within intracytoplasmic lumina (Pap).

A binucleated cell with a neutrophil in an intracytoplasmic lumen between the two nuclei (centre) and several other large neoplastic cells containing variable amounts of cytoplasm and showing large pleomorphic nuclei (Pap).

A small tissue fragment demonstrates the complexity of vacuolization that can be seen in epithelioid haemangioendothelioma, with red cells and neutrophils in some vacuoles, and a striking “cell-within-a-cell” morphology, with cells apparently wrapped in larger cells. The nuclei vary in size, degree of pleomorphism and coarse chromatin, and prominence of nucleoli (Pap).

Abundant, vacuolated cytoplasm with enlarged pleomorphic nuclei is seen. Distinct intracytoplasmic lumina are present, and the neoplastic cells on the left side of the field appear to form an intercellular lumen (Giemsa).

A minute tissue fragment consisting of large cells with often abundant cytoplasm, marked anisonucleosis, irregular nuclear contours, and prominent nucleoli – features that overlap with those of adenocarcinoma, which is often in the different diagnosis (Giemsa).
Strong nuclear staining for CAMTA1, which is a surrogate marker for CAMTA1::WWTR1 fusion, is a reliable diagnostic marker for epithelioid haemangioendothelioma (cell block, ICC).
